                        Transition operation · startup, shutdown, cleaning, campaigns and load following on E-101

                        Teaching slide deck · why E-101 has transitions, startup and shutdown in order with the reasons, the vacuum after a steam cut, cleaning and storage, set-point campaigns and load following, all run on the model.
                        Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                        Follows the course lecture on operating during transitions (Process Operation, with the startup workshop). The Operating windows tab looks at steady states; a transition is the planned transient between an initial and a final condition. Every trend below was produced by running a copy of this simulator's model through the transition with a script (cold startup, shutdown, trip and restart, set-point and load changes); the live plant is not touched. The graded procedures stay on the Exercises tab.

                        1 Transitions · 2 Before startup · 3 Startup · 4 Shutdown and ESD · 5 Vacuum and restart · 6 Cleaning and maintenance · 7 Set-point campaigns · 8 Load following · 9 What makes transitions hard

                        1 · What a transition is, and which ones E-101 has

                        Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. They need their own procedures, strategies, process structure and sometimes extra equipment, because the plant was designed for the steady state. E-101 sits between two plants it does not control: the flash-steam header of an upstream plant and the boiler house that takes the heated BFW. Every E-101 transition therefore touches its neighbours.

                        KindWhen it happensOn E-101Part

                        2 · Before startup: the plant is made ready

                        Done before the procedure starts (lecture list, applied to E-101):

                          Extra equipment and features that exist mainly for transitions:

                          ItemWhy a transition needs it

                          3 · Startup from cold: the order and the reasons

                          Initial condition (the cold snapshot the simulator uses): BFW pumps stopped, XV-100 closed and the SIS reset, all controllers in MAN at 0 %, the shell cold and full of air at atmospheric pressure, metal at 25 °C.

                          No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                          How fast may the steam come in? The same script was run from the cold snapshot (pump start, FIC-101 to 100 m³/h, V-104 open, XV-100 opened with FIC-104 in MAN at 5 %) with different ways of raising the FIC-104 output, handing over to cascade when TT-101 reached 66 °C. The model's water-hammer rule is metal below °C while more than kg/h of steam enters (or steam onto a flooded shell).

                          Events in the selected run

                          4 · Shutdown and emergency shutdown: remove the heat first, keep the heat sink last

                          No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                          5 · The shell goes to vacuum when the steam stops, so every restart needs venting

                          Steam that stops flowing keeps condensing on the cold tubes: the shell pressure collapses below atmospheric within seconds. The trap cannot discharge against the return header, and VB-101 opens to let air in (it protects the shell from collapse and lets the condensate drain). The shell is then full of air again, exactly as at a cold start. The restart after an ESD with BFW kept flowing was scripted twice, with the same warm-up and ramp:

                          6 · Cleaning, regeneration and maintenance transitions

                          Heat-transfer surfaces foul and need cleaning; strainers fill; traps, valves and transmitters need maintenance. The lecture's three strategies: parallel equipment (one is cleaned while the other runs), storage (the neighbours run from a tank while the unit is out), or shutdown. On E-101 one side is a utility (flash steam) and the other is the product delivered to the boiler house (BFW), so the questions are different on each side.

                          Cleaning or maintenance on E-101WhyWhat changesHazards and how they are handledStrategy

                          Blocked operation on a bypass

                          While the trap line is out (V-101 and V-102 closed), condensate can only leave through the trap bypass V-103, a hand valve with no steam seal: too little opening and the shell floods, too much and live steam blows through to the return header. This is a temporary, attended operation: an operator stays at the valve, the time is kept short, and the steam loss and hotwell are watched. It is a transition in its own right, with an entry step (line up the bypass, then isolate the trap) and an exit step (trap back in service, then close the bypass).

                          How big must the storage be?

                          E-101 has no parallel exchanger and no buffer of heated BFW. To keep the boilers fed while it is out, either stored BFW covers the outage (holdup time V/F ≥ outage time) or the BFW bypasses the bundle (recommended addition) and the boiler house heats it with its own steam.

                          7 · Set-point campaigns: changing the outlet temperature

                          When the same equipment serves different needs it runs in blocks of steady operation separated by transitions; material made during the transition is off-specification, so transitions should be expedited. Suppose the boiler house asks for a lower BFW temperature (70 → 63 °C) for a period. Off-spec time is counted while TT-101 is more than 1 °C from the new target:

                          What a lower outlet does to the shell pressure and the trap

                          E-101 has a fixed area, so less duty means a lower condensing temperature, and the shell pressure floats down with it. The trap needs a pressure difference to the return header; below a certain outlet the trap cannot pass the condensate, the hotwell rises into the tubes and the flooded area takes over part of the control (a stall). Steady states from the model, cascade in service:

                          8 · Load following: the boiler house sets the BFW rate

                          A supplier that feeds consumers without storage must follow the load in time. E-101 has no tank between it and the boilers: when the boiler house raises its demand, FIC-101 follows and the steam must follow the water. The FIC-101 set point was moved 100 → 120 m³/h at several ramp rates with TIC-101 in cascade:

                          Lecture's industrial practice (steam systems)Same idea on E-101

                          9 · Batch processes, and what makes transitions hard

                          Batch operation (all material at the start) and semi-batch (some added later) never reach a steady state: every batch is a transition, used for small quantities, high purity or long residence times, with storage between batch and continuous sections. E-101 is continuous, so its transitions are the ones above.

                            References: course lecture on operating during transitions and the process startup workshop (Process Operation); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; general steam-system practice for heat exchangers (venting of non-condensables, trap selection, vacuum breakers, water-hammer prevention); TEMA practice for exchanger cleaning.

                            Process reliability · how long E-101 delivers hot BFW between outages, and how to make it run longer

                            Teaching slide deck · reliability, failure rate and availability, series, parallel, standby and k-out-of-N structures on E-101, the fouling-driven cleaning interval, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost.
                            Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                            Follows the course material on reliability (operability in process design, the reliability chapter and its workshop; failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series, parallel and k-of-N models, critical items). This tab treats reliability of production: an outage of E-101 costs heat and, if the BFW stops, the boilers' feed. Reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand, SIL, layers) is on the LOPA tab. Failure rates marked "course generic" are all-modes values from the course data; everything marked "assumed" is a teaching value, not plant data.

                            1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 E-101 as a series system · 5 Design for reliability · 6 Fouling and the cleaning interval · 7 Inventory · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost · 10 Steam-heater reliability audit

                            1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                            TermDefinitionOn E-101

                            Availability is not reliability. A heater that trips twelve times a year but restarts in fifteen minutes each time has high availability and poor reliability; every trip is a vacuum, an air-filled shell, a vent-and-warm-up restart and a cold spell for the boilers. The course example: three years of the same plant with uptimes 6815, 7612 and 8471 h of 8760 h.

                            2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                            Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time divided by the items still working. Over life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most real equipment does not follow the full bathtub (reliability-centred maintenance studies found six patterns, most without wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                            R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

                            At t = MTTF only 37 % survive (63.2 % have failed). Course example: λ = 0.0001 /h → MTTF 10 000 h; R(5000 h) = e−0.5 = 0.61. The Weibull model R(t) = exp[−(t/η)β] covers all three regions with the shape β:

                            3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                            A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. All formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

                            StructureWorks whenReliabilityMTTF (identical elements, λ each)E-101 example

                            4 · E-101 as a series system: what stops the hot BFW, and how often

                            For production every element in the chain pump → BFW valve and flow loop → tubes → steam supply and FV-104 → condensate removal → temperature loop → trips must work, so E-101 is a series system: λsys = Σ λi × fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop the unit (a spurious trip, lost flow, lost heating). Each outage costs the repair or switching time plus a restart: . Toggle design changes and watch outages, availability and the Pareto.

                            5 · Design for reliability

                            Lecture principleWhat it meansE-101 as builtGap or recommendation

                            "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized trap cycles hard and wears out; an undersized one floods the shell at low pressure. An oversized pump runs far left of its best-efficiency point and fails on seals and bearings. On E-101 the lesson runs the other way too: FV-104 is sized for design with little margin, so fouling and load both reach its travel limit early (part 6 and the Transition operation tab).

                            6 · Operating for reliability: fouling and the cleaning interval

                            The lecture's trade-off: a short-term gain (running on, pushing a variable toward a constraint) against long-term life. On E-101 the slow killer is scale inside the tubes. As the fouling resistance grows, the controller keeps 70 °C by raising the shell pressure, until FV-104 runs out of travel. The model was run to steady state (owRun, cascade in service) at increasing scale severity; pick the load and the header pressure, set a fouling rate, and read the cleaning interval:

                            7 · Reliability through inventory: TK-101 hold-up

                            A tank between an unreliable unit and the next one lets the next unit keep running while the first is repaired. With the upstream unit's repair time exponentially distributed (mean MTTR) and a hold-up time τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered by the tank is 1 − e−τ/MTTR, so Rsys = R2[R1 + (1 − R1)(1 − e−τ/MTTR)]. For E-101 the upstream unit is the water treatment that fills TK-101 (outside the simulator), and unit 2 is E-101 itself, with R2 taken live from part 4.

                            Inventory has a price: tank cost and space, water that must be kept deaerated or chemically treated, and heat lost from stored hot water. The engineer places inventory next to the unreliable unit and sizes it for that unit's repair time; a tank after E-101 would need to hold heated BFW (Transition operation tab, storage calculator).

                            8 · Maintenance for reliability

                            StrategyIdeaE-101 items that suit it

                            9 · Life-cycle cost: how many BFW pumps?

                            Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability analysis the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, failure frequency, the cost of each failure (repair, lost production, restart) and the extra equipment for redundancy. The course example asks how many pumps to install. Costs below are assumed teaching values; the restart time comes from the Transition operation tab.

                            Efficiency · where E-101's flash steam goes, and what it is worth to the boiler

                            Teaching slide deck · efficiency and its place among the priorities, E-101 by the direct and indirect method, the value of BFW preheat to the boiler, venting, traps, fouling, pump energy, constraint pushing and an energy dashboard, all on the E-101 model.
                            Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                            Curves and tables marked "model" are steady states of this simulator (a copy of the model run to steady state with the trips switched off, TIC-101 in cascade on FIC-104 unless stated). Live tables read the running simulator. Prices, the boiler efficiency and the other economic values are assumed teaching values: change them in the box below and every part updates.

                            1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 Chains multiply · 3 E-101 efficiency now · 4 BFW preheat and the boiler · 5 Venting · 6 Steam traps · 7 Fouling · 8 Pump energy · 9 Push toward the constraint · 10 Energy monitoring
                            Economic basis (assumed teaching values)

                            1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                            Efficiency (in operation, the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: the product delivered at the rate and quality needed with less energy, raw material and effluent, and less environmental impact. For energy: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ energy input.

                            For E-101 the useful output is the heat picked up by the BFW, F·cp·(Tout − Tin); the input is the energy the flash steam brings. Four ways to improve it: design with the right capacities (pump, valve, surface); use the existing equipment in the most efficient way (vent, trap, clean tubes); choose a better process structure (recover the flash steam at all, return the condensate); choose the best operating conditions inside the window (part 9).

                            Efficiency is not first: an operator never trades a higher priority for it. Opening the vent wastes steam but protects the surface and the tubes; keeping BFW flowing after a steam trip wastes nothing yet matters more than anything on this tab.

                            PriorityObjectiveOn E-101

                            2 · Chains multiply: flash steam → BFW → boiler fuel

                            Efficiencies in series multiply. The lecture example is electricity: boiler 90 % × turbo-generator 40 % × transmission 90 % = 32.4 %. For E-101 the chain runs the other way and ends in a division: every kilowatt put into the BFW is a kilowatt the boiler does not have to raise from fuel, and the boiler needs 1/ηboiler kW of fuel for each kilowatt it adds to the water. Recovered low-grade steam therefore saves more fuel than its own heat.

                            3 · E-101 efficiency now: direct and indirect method

                            Direct method: η = heat picked up by the BFW ÷ energy brought by the steam, both from meters (FIC-101, TT-101, TI-103 for the water; FIC-104 and PI-100 → Tsat for the steam). Indirect method: η = 100 % − losses, each loss taken from the model's own states (vent steam Wvent, live steam through the trap, bypass or drain Wsl, steam condensed on leaking BFW). Two bases for "energy in": the latent basis Win·λ(Ts), which is what a steam heater is designed to use, and the enthalpy basis Win·(hsteam − hmake-up) above the BFW inlet temperature, which also counts the heat that leaves in the condensate. Both are computed live from the running simulator.

                            4 · The value of BFW preheat to the boiler

                            Each °C of preheat in E-101 is heat the boiler does not have to supply: fuel saved ≈ F·ρ·cp·ΔT ÷ ηboiler. The flow and water properties are the model's; the boiler efficiency and fuel price are the assumed basis above. The CO₂ factor is an assumed natural-gas value.

                            5 · Venting: steam lost against blanketing and the FV-104 margin

                            Gas that does not condense collects at the far end of the shell and blankets tubes; TIC-101 then opens FV-104 and raises the shell pressure to push the same heat through less surface. A vent removes the gas but blows live steam with it. The model runs below (3 h each, so the gas inventory settles) sweep the air vent V-104 from closed to 50 % at four gas loads (share of the fault's full rate), and compare two design alternatives on the P&ID: rev B, a fixed restriction orifice RO-101 around V-104, and rev C, an automatic air vent AAV-101 that opens only when its line runs cool (TI-102). This is a design trade-off, not one right setting: the right answer depends on how much gas the steam carries, and that changes.

                            6 · Steam traps: a failed-open trap, and what a trap survey is worth

                            A trap that fails open passes live steam to the condensate return. TIC-101 does not see it: the outlet stays on set point and FIC-104 simply rises, so the loss appears only in a steam balance or a trap survey. Model runs with ST-101 failing open by different amounts:

                            Across a site the same mechanism repeats at every trap. Survey calculator: steam lost through one failed-open trap by the Napier orifice relation, W = Cd × 51.4 × A[in²] × P[psia] lb/h (assumed discharge coefficient), at the trap's inlet pressure.

                            7 · Fouling: scale inside the tubes

                            Scale adds a resistance in series with the tube-side film, so UA falls and PDI-109 rises. At first nothing is lost on the latent basis: the controller simply raises the shell pressure (and FV-104) to push the same heat through the dirtier surface. The cost is margin, and once FV-104 runs out, outlet shortfall, which the boiler must make up with fuel. Model runs at design flow and header pressure:

                            8 · Pump energy: recycle and throttling against a variable-speed drive

                            P-101A runs at constant speed. FIC-101 sets the flow by throttling FV-101A, and FV-101B opens by the same amount FV-101A closes, so part of the pumped water only goes round the recycle. Both burn pump energy. A variable-speed drive (VSD) could set the flow by speed with FV-101A wide open (affinity laws: flow ∝ speed, head ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³). The hydraulics below solve the model's own pump, valve and tube equations; pump, motor and drive efficiencies and the electricity price are assumed.

                            9 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraint

                            Many settings do not touch safety or quality but do move the fuel bill; the best value usually sits against a constraint, and how close you can go depends on variability. For E-101 a hotter outlet saves boiler fuel (part 4). Which constraint binds? The temperature limits downstream, or the steam supply through FV-104? Move the set point and the variability and see.

                            Industrial practice: reduce variability first, then move the set point; optimise slowly (a fast optimiser upsets the boiler house), from a model when one exists and from careful plant tests when not; change the alarm limits and the operating window through management of change, never by habit.

                            10 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables for E-101

                            A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific energy consumption against its benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it. Live from the simulator (vent and trap losses come from the model; in a plant they need a vent-line thermometer such as TI-102 on rev C, trap monitors or a periodic survey):

                            Key energy variableTargetNowWhy it matters

Marlin, Process Operability class materials; US DOE steam system tip sheets (steam traps, vents, condensate return); ASME PTC 4 (boiler efficiency, direct and indirect methods).

                            Open the deck ↗Same folder (offline / GitHub Pages)

                            Written for this simulator's E-101: tags, alarm limits and trip settings are read from the page's own alarm list and trip constants when the tab loads. Numbers marked "model" come from scripted runs on copies of the E-101 model (an expert following each SOP). These SOPs are teaching documents in a standard format; a real unit's SOPs are approved under its own management system (PSM, MOC) and signed off by operations, process and safety.

                            1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                            1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                            A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (start-up order, operating window, trips, venting) into actions an operator can follow under pressure.

                            Process safety management requires written procedures for each operating phase (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f)): initial startup, normal operations, temporary operations, emergency shutdown (including who decides and when), emergency operations, normal shutdown, and startup after a turnaround or an emergency shutdown; plus the operating limits with the consequences of deviation and the steps to correct or avoid it, the safety and health considerations (hazards, precautions, exposure control), and the safety systems and their functions. Procedures must be readily available, certified as current each year, and cover safe work practices such as lockout/tagout and line opening.

                            6 · The life of an SOP

                            Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures in the Exercises tab run the same steps) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with every deviation reported → review after any change (management of change), after an incident or near miss, and at the fixed interval (certified annually under PSM), then revise and re-issue.

                            References: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f) Operating procedures and (j) mechanical integrity; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 Control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout); CCPS, Guidelines for Writing Effective Operating and Maintenance Procedures; Thai Department of Industrial Works notification on process safety management.

                            1 · How an EPC project is organised

                            An EPC contractor Engineers, Procures and Constructs the plant. Engineering is split into disciplines, each writing its own documents but always from the documents of the discipline before it: Process fixes what the unit must do (PFD, heat and material balance, P&ID, relief basis); Mechanical, Instrumentation and Electrical turn that into equipment that can be bought; Safety reviews the design (HAZOP, LOPA) and sends recommendations back to every discipline; Commissioning turns the documents into tests and a start-up. Every document has a number, a revision and a status, and lives in one document register. When a discipline finds that two documents disagree or a value is missing, it raises an engineering query instead of guessing: the query log is how the project keeps its numbers consistent.

                            Document numbers: BFWH-V1-<discipline>-<type>-nnn, e.g. BFWH-V1-EE-LL-001 = unit BFW heater ver 1, Electrical, Load List, number 001. Discipline codes: .

                            Relief & vent · relief load basis and relief device sizing for E-101

                            Teaching slide deck · Relief & vent — the ideas of this tab taught in three parts with interactive slides built on this unit's numbers.
                            Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                            The relief study is the process engineer's proof that every way the E-101 shell or tubes can be over- or under-pressured has a device that can pass the load. It reads the cases from the model and the Design tab, sizes the devices with the API 520 relations and lists them in a register. Relief is layer 4 of the protection: the other layers are on the Safety layers, LOPA and SRS of SIF tabs.

                            1 What the study delivers · 2 Scenario screening · 3 API 520 sizing · 4 Device register · 5 Inlet and outlet · 6 Checks and queries

                            1 · What the relief study delivers

                            • Scenario screening (API 521): every cause of overpressure or vacuum is listed and judged credible or not, with a reason. A case that is not credible is written down too, so the next reviewer sees it was considered.
                            • Relief loads: for each credible case, the flow the device must pass and the relieving pressure and temperature (set + 10 % overpressure).
                            • Sizing (API 520 Part I): required orifice area → the next standard API 526 orifice letter; the largest credible load for that device governs.
                            • Datasheet and register: one line per device: set pressure, case, size, discharge location, status (existing, recommended, HOLD).
                            • Discharge routing: to a safe location (steam and hot water here; no flare is needed), checked for inlet loss and back-pressure (API 520 Part II).

                            The model has no PSV. The pressures in section 2 are what a relief device would see; they come from model runs with the trips disabled (ENG.D.runs). Design pressures and the header maximum are the Design tab assumptions (shell 350, tubes 1 100, header maximum 300 kPa g).

                            2 · Scenario screening for the E-101 shell (PSV-100) and the tube side

                            Model runs behind the "Model" column (copies of the model from the design snapshot, trips disabled, no relief device):

                            A cause whose pressure source sits below the set pressure (the header at its maximum, the BFW against a closed outlet on the shell side) gives no relief load: it is pressure-limited. Only fire, tube rupture and a header let-down failure beyond the assumed maximum can push the shell past 350 kPa g; thermal expansion and vacuum need their own small devices.

                            3 · API 520 sizing: steam and liquid

                            Steam relief (API 520 Part I, Napier form) · case
                            Liquid relief: tube rupture (API 520 Part I)

                            API 526 standard effective orifice areas:

                            4 · Relief device register

                            VB-101 vacuum breaker: in-breathing after XV-100 closes

                            At 100 % of the condensing rate the breaker is large: this is why a shell rated for full vacuum is often cheaper than a breaker sized for the worst case (HAZOP R14). Air drawn in must be vented at the next start (R21).

                            Tube-side thermal relief (TRV, recommended by HAZOP R05)

                            Vents: V-104 on 1"-VT-101 at the far end of the shell; rev B RO-101 passes a continuous 0.5–1 % of the steam, rev C AAV-101 opens when the vent line (TI-102) runs cool. Every discharge (PSV-100, RD-100, V-104, V-103, V-105) goes to a safe location (HAZOP R17).

                            5 · Inlet loss and back-pressure of PSV-100

                            Rules: the pressure loss from the shell to the PSV inlet at the rated capacity stays within 3 % of the set pressure (otherwise the valve chatters); the built-up back-pressure on a conventional valve stays within 10 % of set (otherwise Kb falls and the set pressure shifts; use a balanced bellows). Incompressible estimate with the density at each end, adequate when the result is a few per cent.

                            1 · What instrumentation & control engineering delivers

                            2 · Instrument list (index)

                            ·

                            Ranges are the DCS ranges of the model (controller ranges from the loops, indicator scales from the DCS faceplates); normal values are the design snapshot; alarm and trip settings are the model's alarm table and SIS I-100. Recommended additions come from the HAZOP (R02, R10, R12) and P&ID note 7; their ranges are assumed. Fail positions: FV-101A FO, FV-104 FC, XV-100 FC, FV-101B TBC.

                            3 · I/O schedule and SIS independence

                            Spare: 20 % installed spare per system and type (assumed), rounded up. Pump run status and start / stop count two channels each (MCC interface assumed).

                            Independence rule: a safety instrumented function reads its own sensor, not the transmitter of the control loop or alarm whose failure it protects against. Otherwise one failed transmitter both causes the upset and blinds the trip.

                            4 · Worked example: ranging the FE-101 orifice and checking the span

                            An orifice gives ΔP ∝ Q². The transmitter is calibrated in ΔP and the DCS takes the square root: flow % = √(ΔP %). Near zero flow a small ΔP error is a large flow error, so an orifice loop is usable only down to about a quarter of its span (4:1 flow turndown, assumed). FT-101 serves FIC-101 (0–160 m³/h) and, today, the FSLL-101 trip at 30 m³/h.

                            Range checker: choose an instrument; normal, alarms and trip as % of the calibrated span (good practice: inside 10–90 %).

                            2 · Electrical load list

                            Each consumer is listed with its rated power, the power it actually absorbs, the load factor (absorbed ÷ rated), the efficiency and power factor, and the duty: continuous, intermittent or standby. The maximum demand applies a diversity factor to each row: 1 for continuous, 0 for the standby pump (only one BFW pump runs at a time), a low value for socket outlets.

                            Values marked assumed are not vendor data.

                            3 · Worked example: P-101A motor rating

                            4 · Cable sizing calculator (400 V, three-phase, DOL motor)

                            A motor cable must (1) carry the full-load current after derating for ambient temperature and grouping, (2) keep the voltage drop while running within 5 %, and (3) keep the voltage drop during a direct-on-line (DOL) start, at about 6 × the full-load current and a low power factor, within 15 %, so the motor can still accelerate. The smallest size meeting all three is selected.

                            Current ratings and resistances are typical values for copper conductors with PVC insulation, multicore cable on a tray in air (three loaded conductors), for teaching only; the project uses the cable manufacturer's tables and the installation method of the cable route. Resistance is corrected from 20 °C to the operating temperature by the factor shown; reactance 0.08 Ω/km assumed.

                            1 · The project phases after design

                            Design ends with documents; the plant exists only after these phases. Each ends with a certificate that the next phase relies on, and each is organised by system (BFW, steam, condensate, …) rather than by discipline, because a system is what can be tested and handed over on its own.

                            2 · Procurement packages

                            Equipment and bulk are bought in packages, each from one supplier, against the data sheets of the discipline that specified it. Long-lead items (here the heater, the pumps, the SIS valve and the DCS/SIS) are ordered first because their delivery sets the construction schedule. The inspection level (assumed) says how closely the buyer follows manufacture: from an inspector at every hold point (level 1) to certificates only (level 4). Lead times are assumed, typical ranges.

                            3 · Inspection and testing

                            The factory acceptance test (FAT) proves the item at the vendor's works before it ships; the site acceptance test (SAT) proves it again after installation. A hydrotest fills a pressure part with water at 1.3 × its design pressure (assumed code factor, no temperature correction) to prove strength and tightness before it ever sees steam.

                            SIS proof tests before start-up. Each safety instrumented function is tested end to end before the first steam is admitted, and again every year (proof-test interval in the SRS tab). The trip set points are read from the model.

                            4 · Pre-commissioning checklist (tick as you go)

                            One list per system. Ticks are kept only while this page is open (they are not saved). The system is ready for commissioning when its bar reaches 100 %.

                            Incident cases · what real steam, condensate and exchanger accidents teach about E-101

                            Teaching slide deck · Incident cases — the ideas of this tab taught in three parts with interactive slides built on this unit's numbers.
                            Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)
                            1 Why incidents · 2 Timeline · 3 The cases · 4 Where on E-101 · 5 Barrier matrix · 6 Self-check · 7 Videos · 8 Sources

                            Eight published accidents on steam mains, condensate systems, feed-water piping and shell-and-tube heat exchangers, the equipment E-101 is made of. Facts are taken from the investigation reports and summaries listed under each case (CSB, NRC, HSE, the operators' and regulators' releases; Wikipedia only as a second source); where sources differ, the figure used is the one in the first source listed. The lessons for E-101 are the author's reading of those findings against this unit's design, tags and HAZOP recommendations; they are not part of any investigation.

                            1 · Why study incidents, and how to read a case

                            Low-pressure steam looks harmless. It is not: a slug of condensate driven by steam, a vessel thinned by oxygen, a shell or a tube bundle blocked in with heat on it, or hot water flashing from a burst pipe has killed people in every decade. The same few patterns repeat across industries, and every one of them has a place on E-101.

                            Read every case in three steps:

                            1. What happened: the sequence, in time order, from the first abnormal condition to the consequence.
                            2. Why: the immediate cause (the physical failure) and the barriers that failed or were missing. Two kinds are tagged: the six protection layers of the Safety layers tab (L1 process control, L2 alarms and operator, L3 SIS, L4 relief, L5 physical protection and isolation, L6 emergency response) and the management-system elements that keep those layers alive (change management, hazard study and its actions, inspection and mechanical integrity, procedures and training, permit and isolation, layout and siting, safety culture).
                            3. So what for E-101: the same equipment, line or task on this unit, its tag or line number, what already protects it and what is recommended, and the exercise in this simulator where you can feel the same physics.
                            Swiss cheese, not one cause. In every case below several barriers were weak at the same time. Closing any one of the holes would have stopped the event or cut its consequence. Look for the holes that exist today on E-101, not for the person to blame.

                            The Try it buttons load the matching training exercise, Think EQUIPPED case or procedure and open the DCS console. Doing so replaces the current session, and the case text tells you which upset you are about to meet.

                            2 · Timeline

                            Click a point to open the case. Bar height = people killed; dot size = people injured (log scale).

                            5 · Barrier matrix

                            ● barrier failed, missing or bypassed (a direct cause, or a cause of the size of the consequence); ○ a weakness the investigation named as contributing. Counts are computed from the case data. Click a case to open it.
